Its name derives from the lyra of the Byzantine empire and it may have evolved from it, being comparable to the rebab of the Islamic empire of the time. The ninth-century Persian geographer Ibn Khordadbeh listed the lyra as a typical Byzantine instrument. The Byzantine lyra spread westwards, and in the eleventh and twelfth centuries European writers used "bowed fiddle" and "lyra" interchangeably. Later European bowed instruments divided into the arm-held family of the arm lyra and the lap-held family of the leg lyra; the leg lyra was important in the Renaissance, but the louder arm-held family gradually replaced it.

The lijerica is a bowed instrument from Dalmatia in Croatia and parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321-71. The body is pear-shaped, with three strings, played with a bow. Its name comes from the Byzantine bowed instrument the lyra, from which it may have evolved. It is often used in traditional folk music, to accompany the local linđo dance; it also appears in modern music, for example in the hands of Mate Bulić.
